Section 144 imposed in Rawalpindi district for a month over 'threat to law and order'. The Rawalpindi deputy commissioner on Saturday announced that Section 144 had been imposed in the district for a period of 30 days, over threats to sensitive installations and other critical infrastructure. Section 144 is a provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure which empowers local authorities to ban public gatherings such as rallies, processions and sit-ins, as well as the open display of weapons. It has been imposed amid the PTI’s long march , which has so far remained within Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, but had initially announced to move towards the federal capital. The KP chief minister reiterated today that he would lead the convoy towards Islamabad. According to a notification seen by Dawn , the District Intelligence Committee (DIC) in a meeting today warned the DC of an “imminent threat” within the district to sensitive installations, major roads and other infrastructure “which may pose a serious risk to human life, public property, and the overall peace and order of the district”. “The DIC has reported specific intelligence suggesting that certain groups and elements are actively mobilising with intentions to disturb the law and order situation through large gatherings, protests, and disruptive assemblies,” the notification read. Moreover, the committee indicated that these elements may mobilise “individuals with the potential to engage in violent actions” against soft targets and near key installations and other sensitive sites. Imposing Section 144, DC retired Captain Nadeem Nasir prohibited public gatherings of more than five people, as well as the open display of weapons, improvised explosives, spikes, laden batons, gulails, ball bearings, petrol bombs, or other instruments that could cause physical harm. It also banned the use of drones and any attempts to “remove any restriction” imposed by the police to regulate assemblies and traffic. The order is set to expire on Nov 8. Section 144 has already been imposed in several parts of the country, with Islamabad imposing the provision for two months in a notification dated September 18. The order prohibited gatherings of five or more people, as well as processions, rallies and demonstrations, at any public place within the revenue limits of the district, including the Red Zone. Similarly, Section 144 is in force in Lahore until Oct 15, with the order citing serious threats to public peace, tranquillity and the safety of life and property. According to a notification issued by the Punjab Home Department, a complete ban was imposed on assemblies, processions and gatherings of five or more persons at public places, roads and open spaces. However, the ban would not apply to wedding ceremonies, funeral prayers, burials, mosques and other places of worship, courts or government institutions.

India's Cockroach Janta Party says thousands detained during New Delhi protest against CEC. Indian police detained the head of the Cockroach Janta Party , as well as thousands of protesters trying to take part in a major demonstration in New Delhi against the country’s election commissioner, the group said on Saturday. The protest is the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision by the Election Commission of India (ECI). CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital, according to a statement from the movement. “They’re being denied access to their lawyers and cut off from all contact with others,” it said, adding the trio had been taken to “an undisclosed location”. The CJP also said that thousands more protesters were detained in New Delhi as they attempted to march to the main Jantar Mantar protest site, defying a massive security clampdown. “More than 15,000 protesters have been detained,” Ajinkya Shinde, a CJP leader, said at a news conference in Delhi. Police did not immediately respond to AFP ’s request for comment on detentions. “We will be back, let them fill up all the jails,” Shinde said. Dozens of protesters shouted anti-government slogans as they were taken away in police vehicles, AFP reporters witnessed. Calls for the ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar to step down have intensified in recent weeks as opposition parties and critics said his commission’s voter-roll revision could disenfranchise millions of constituents and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety, saying the revision was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters. Ahead of the protest, authorities in the capital deployed thousands of police, closed dozens of metro stations, cancelled more than 200 trains and temporarily shut down mobile internet around the protest site. Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel stand guard ahead of a protest by the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner over alleged “special intensive revision” (SIR) voter-roll irregularities, in New Delhi on October 10, 2026. — AFP The demonstrations are widely seen as a reprise of the “cockroach” movement’s mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal. This time, protesters are demanding Kumar’s resignation and a halt to the voter revision exercise. Fresh challenge The accusations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office. Opposition parties have long alleged that legitimate voters are being struck off lists in India, the world’s largest democracy with 1.4 billion people. The issue flared up last month when Indian Express reported that key decisions linked to the revision were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners. The ECI, a constitutional body, says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid. Demonstrators expressed anger on Saturday, telling AFP their right to protest peacefully was being hampered. Saransh, a university graduate, walked several miles after navigating security barricades to get close to the Jantar Mantar protest site. “I am here to protect the constitution,” said the 24-year-old, who gave only one name. “Why do I need permission to peacefully express my opinion?” ‘Keep protesting’ Amnesty International denounced the “lockdown-like restrictions” and leader of the opposition Congress party, Rahul Gandhi, called on young people to continue with the rallies. “Youth of India, I am proud of you. Keep protesting. We are standing with you,” he said. The Hindu reported that more than 5,000 protesters had been detained, although it was not immediately possible to verify that number. Media outlets, including the Scroll and Newslaundry , said their journalists had also been detained briefly. The United Nations’ human rights office urged India to release those “arbitrarily detained” in the protests and expressed concern at reports of mass detentions. BJP spokesman Sambit Patra said on Saturday the CJP had failed in its attempt to spread “anarchy”. “What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story,” he told reporters. The voter list overhaul, which began in 2025, has led to more than 133 million names being excluded from draft rolls, according to Indian media reports citing ECI data. The ECI has said the voter-roll revision identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from voting. Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities. Members of Modi’s party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls. Political analyst Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told AFP the protest comes at a time when Modi appears to be “at his weakest politically and individually”. Though India’s next general elections are not slated until 2029, the country’s most populous state of Uttar Pradesh will go to the polls next year. “I see this becoming a bigger challenge in the coming months,” Mukhopadhyay said.

Global growth set to slow. ISLAMABAD: Global economic growth is projected to slow to 2.6 per cent in 2026 and 2.7pc in 2027, from 2.9pc in 2025, while growth in developing economies is expected to fall to 4pc from 4.7pc, amid mounting technological and policy barriers, according to the Trade and Development Report 2026. The flagship report by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) finds that governments increasingly use industrial, trade, financial, and technology policies to pursue economic and national security objectives. Access to markets and the ability to move into higher-value activities now depend more heavily on technology, finance and geopolitics. Developing countries will be affected unevenly by the reconfiguration of global trade. Some may emerge as alternative suppliers or intermediary hubs, but sustaining these gains will require stronger productive, regulatory and institutional capabilities, the report warns. Global trade reached a record $35 trillion in 2025. Higher trade values in 2026 are being driven by rising prices amid the energy shock. Trade patterns are also shifting, with trade between China and the United States falling by more than 20pc since 2024, while East Asia has expanded trade with both China and North America. Export controls, investment screening and supply-chain conditions are making it harder for new entrants to access strategic sectors. Asia remains the most dynamic exporting region, with intra-Asian merchandise trade rising markedly. South-South trade is also deepening as China and other major Asian exporters increase shipments to emerging markets. On the import side, Asia is expected to record the strongest growth in 2026, followed by North America, where demand for artificial intelligence-related goods has supported overall imports. SMOKERS’ CORNER: False Flags and Credibility. Illustration by Abro Last week, reports emerged that an Israeli plumber had thwarted an alleged attempt by the co-pilot of a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv to hijack/crash the aircraft. Interestingly, as further details were made public, social media platforms were flooded with thousands of posts alleging that the incident was a false flag operation orchestrated by the far-right Israeli government and its allied countries’ intelligence agencies. I will not delve into the numerous anomalies highlighted by sceptics, including those raised by active pilots and aviation experts. Instead, this piece focuses on how false flag tactics have begun to backfire. Over the years, significant evidence has emerged demonstrating that staged pretexts have increasingly transitioned from clandestine exceptions to routine instruments of statecraft. Countries using such tactics rely on certain psychological mechanisms that help set up false flag operations. For example, long before a staged provocation takes place, its success is often guaranteed by the cultural and news narratives that precede it. In many countries, movies, television shows and news broadcasts have conditioned audiences to view specific societies through a narrow, negative lens. By repeatedly depicting these populations through recurring tropes of hostility or violence, mainstream media embeds particular perceptions in the public consciousness. Governments have often used media conditioning and false flag operations to make the public more amenable to their agendas. In an age of information warfare, however, scepticism about official narratives is increasing. And scepticism can be a double-edged sword… In their work Manufacturing Consent, media scholars Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky conceptualised this process through their “propaganda model”, demonstrating how mass media functions as an ideological filter, designed to align public perception with official state policy objectives. Rather than presenting objective facts, modern entertainment and news ecosystems construct artificial frames that prompt ordinary citizens to support aggressive foreign policy agendas. When cultural caricatures of ‘enemy’ societies are continuously reinforced, they generate the precise environment required for staged pretexts and/or false flag operations. If a government or intelligence apparatus seeks to fabricate a pretext for military action, global observers rarely question the official narrative, because the alleged culprit matches the villain archetype they have been conditioned to accept by the media. Back in 1922, the American journalist and author Walter Lippmann observed that people construct their worldviews based on simplified “pictures in their heads” created by media narratives, rendering ‘enemy’ populations vulnerable to instant condemnation whenever a security crisis is reported. This dynamic is illustrated across several geopolitical events. During the run-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Western news outlets and Hollywood routinely depicted Middle Eastern figures through tropes of inherent fanaticism and anti-Western hostility, a phenomenon critically analysed by Edward Said in Orientalism, which showed how cultural production systematically portrays non-Western societies as dangerous. When US and British leaders falsely asserted that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction (WMD), large segments of the public accepted the premise without demanding any serious empirical evidence. The claim naturally aligned with a pre-existing media script. The American media historian Nancy Snow wrote that, across the Cold War, American entertainment and news outlets constantly framed the Soviet Union as a dark, deceitful empire, capable of any atrocity. This persistent framing meant that US covert intelligence operations and exaggerated threats of Soviet terror were accepted almost instantly by a public already conditioned to expect malevolent behaviour from the Soviet regime. However, sometimes, when this tactic is overtly used, the user country can get trapped in its own strategy. For example, the enemy country’s culture may indeed be successfully demonised by propaganda but, eventually, the user country can also start to become widely perceived as a constant engineer of false flag operations. As British media scholar Andrew Hoskins highlights in his research on digital media and conflict, modern hyper-connectivity has fundamentally transformed how the public consumes news during a security crisis. In an era where audiences are routinely exposed to sensationalised reporting, institutional trust has begun to break down. Instead of taking official explanations at face value, global audiences now immediately scrutinise government narratives, moving towards scepticism. This scepticism serves as a vital psychological defence mechanism in an era dominated by ‘information warfare.’ American political scientist Lance Bennett argues that a questioning public is critical for holding power accountable when state actors and media institutions leverage a crisis to manufacture political consent. Questioning official narratives allows citizens to filter out manufactured outrage and demand empirical proof. Indeed, but scepticism can also become a knee-jerk and intellectually lazy exhibition of cynical reflexivity. According to American legal scholar Cass Sunstein, reflexivity that rejects all official accounts can lead to paranoia, where real crises are dismissed as elaborate fabrications. When every high-profile event is instantly dismissed as fake, one crosses into cynicism. Media scholar Renee Hobbs warns that this form of cynicism creates a new cognitive trap. Rather than demanding evidence, individuals simply invert the official narrative to fit their own pre-existing biases. In doing so, the public risks becoming just as easily manipulated by online counter-narratives as they are by official state propaganda. What is truly needed is scepticism that is grounded in deliberate critical thinking. And the good news is that, even amid fierce information wars and state propaganda designed to set the stage for false flag events and despite the knee-jerk reactions that inevitably follow, informed scepticism remains alive. During the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident in the Vietnam War, initial claims by the US government of unprovoked North Vietnamese attacks on American warships were challenged by journalists and naval analysts. Declassified documents later confirmed the attacks were largely fabricated, proving that the US had used them as a pretext for escalating the Vietnam War. Prior to the 1990 Gulf War, testimony claimed Iraqi soldiers were removing Kuwaiti babies from hospital incubators. Sceptical journalists investigated the story and exposed it as a manufactured campaign by the PR firm Hill & Knowlton. In the run-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, UN weapons inspectors Hans Blix and Scott Ritter, along with reporter Seymour Hersh, challenged intelligence claims about yellowcake uranium and mobile bio-labs in Saddam Hussain’s Iraq. Their demand for physical, forensic proof exposed the flawed WMD narrative woven by the US and UK governments. The manner in which a country’s narrative machinery demonises an adversary to set the stage for false flags has become too predictable a tactic to ignore. Recently, Israel and India have landed in this situation. The frequent reliance on demonising narratives, paired with a global public that increasingly demands empirical proof, has repeatedly forced both countries to present ‘evidence’ that many independent observers find deeply unconvincing. When official explanations fall short under critical scrutiny, it fuels scepticism and solidifies the belief that state propaganda is being actively deployed to justify not-very-pleasant strategic objectives. PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed on Saturday put district police on alert for possible violent protests and sabotage in the event of the federal government imposing an emergency in the province, emphasising caution in the use of force. A notification issued by the IGP’s office outlined guidelines for handling protests and warned that miscreants and anti-state elements could exploit demonstrations to incite violence and carry out sabotage activities. “To protect lives and property and prevent sabotage during protests, DPOs, sub-divisional police officers and station house officers should personally monitor all protests within their respective jurisdictions,” it said. The notification said district police must ensure that sufficient personnel were made available to SDPOs and SHOs to maintain order during protests. “The deployment should include anti-riot squads equipped with anti-riot gear, an adequate supply of gas guns and shells checked and verified for use by reserve inspectors or moharrars, special squads of unarmed personnel to identify and apprehend troublemakers and violent protesters, and plainclothes personnel deployed to identify violent protesters, troublemakers and saboteurs. Armed personnel should be deployed only at important or suitable points in extremely urgent situations.” IGP issues guidelines for handling violent protests, stresses caution in use of force The police chief directed SHOs to identify vulnerable locations along protest routes and deploy sufficient personnel to protect them. “Such places may include police stations and police offices, government buildings, petrol stations, banks, shopping centres, important highways/roads and any other sensitive installations,” the notification said. The notification said DPOs could require protest organisers to obtain a licence for an assembly or protest under Section 84 of the KP Police Act, 2017, or any other law or regulation in force, if they considered a breach of the peace likely. According to the guidelines, a DPO, SDPO or SHO could stop a procession that violated the conditions of a licence granted under Section 84 of the KP Police Act, 2017, and order it or any assembly violating such conditions to disperse. “Any procession or assembly, which neglects or refuses to obey any order given Under-Section 85 Sub-Section (I) of Police Act, 2017 or any other law in force shall be deemed an unlawful assembly.” The notification said DPOs could issue appropriate directions, instructions or guidelines to regulate protests and ensure public safety. In the event of violence, they could also take necessary legal action. It added that any police officer could temporarily close or regulate a street or public place by erecting barriers or using other means to prevent people or vehicles from entering an area for security reasons, as provided under Section 88 of the KP Police Act, 2017. According to the notification, during peaceful protests and roadblocks, police should exercise maximum restraint and avoid using force. Protesters should be engaged in negotiations by the senior-most police officer available at the scene, who should try to persuade them to disperse peacefully. It said to prevent serious disorder, a breach of law or imminent danger to life and property, SDPOs, SHOs or the senior-most officer present at the scene could order the appropriate use of force after assessing the situation and declaring the assembly unlawful. The notification said the senior-most supervisory police officer during protests would determine the type and extent of force to be used to disperse an unlawful assembly. “When it is required to use force as per law, its application shall be of minimum essential standard,” the notification said. It emphasised that the use of force should be graduated, starting at the minimum level and increasing only as necessary. In the first phase, violent protesters should be clearly warned before force was used. According to the notification, if necessary, tear-gas shells or grenades should be used from a safe distance to disperse protesters. Rubber-bullet guns and paper-ball guns could also be used against violent protesters from a safe distance. “In the second phase, if the situation requires, the violent protesters may be stopped with baton charge by using the anti-riot gear. The special unarmed squad will be activated to apprehend the violent protesters and take appropriate legal action,” it said. The notification said in cases of extreme violence and an imminent threat to life and property, aerial firing could be conducted by special armed personnel or squads, but only on the directions of the senior-most officer present at the scene. It added that if a person carried a firearm or any article covered under Section 86(1) of the KP Police Act, 2017, the police could seize it and take legal action against the carrier under Section 148 of the Pakistan Penal Code, the notification said. “Extreme caution shall be used while using the force against protesters to avert damage to life and property. Anti-riot squad or the personnel entrusted with use of force shall be properly equipped with anti-riot gear to avoid damage/casualties to life of all concerned,” it said. The notification said the SHO should arrange video recording of the entire protest or procession, preferably through professional cameramen. In the event of a law and order situation, DPOs should ensure briefings, rehearsals and reporting, and issue instructions strictly in accordance with OG-9/2013. “Prior consultation and coordination should be carried out at all supervisory levels with key stakeholders, including the district administration, law enforcement agencies and other relevant bodies,” it said. Sri Lankan vet returns home amid concerns over Madhubala’s health. KARACHI: Sri Lankan wildlife health specialist Dr Buddhika Bandara, who had joined efforts to save Madhubala on Friday, left for home the same day under unclear circumstances, raising concern over Safari Park’s administrative affairs as well as the ongoing health crisis confronting the ailing elephant, it emerged on Saturday. Sources told Dawn that local authorities had not informed the visiting Sri Lankan expert that he would be working with Dr Amir Khalil of the global animal welfare organisation Four Paws at Safari Park. “It seems this situation damaged the trust between the two parties, forcing him to leave quietly. Madhubala’s deteriorating condition must have shocked him, too,” shared an official, adding that Dr Bandara’s hesitation to speak at Friday’s presser surprised many journalists who had requested him several times to share his clinical observations of Madhubala. The sources also expressed concern over the fact that the Safari Park authorities kept Four Paws out for over a year — a critical time during which Madhubala received TB treatment and later developed multiple infections and acute weakness —and then sought its help just three weeks ago when Madhubala’s condition worsened. KMC spokesperson says Dr Bandara left due to death of a family member in Colombo Responding to these concerns, Karachi Metropolitan Corporation’s spokesperson Daniyal Siyal said that Dr Bandara had been monitoring Madhubala’s TB treatment online since his first visit over a year ago. “He had to leave due to the sudden death of his family member in Colombo. Even last month, he was in touch with us. Last year, he stayed with us for 17 days [for Madhubala’s treatment] and this time, his stay was planned for at least a week,” he explained. All support was being extended to Dr Khalil, he added. The foreign experts were invited by local authorities after Safari Park vets had failed to diagnose the factors behind Madhubala’s ongoing health crisis. The female African elephant has experienced drastic weight loss in recent months and collapsed twice in her enclosure. According to Dr Khalil, multiple bacterial and parasitic infections and the weakness that followed treatment for tuberculosis have caused Madhubala to lose significant weight. Additionally, she seems to suffer from a linear fracture in the carpal joint. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

PM takes notice of student’s suicide over visa fraud. ISLAMABAD: The death of student Laiba Aijaz on Friday drew the attention of the government, with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif meeting the Islamabad police chief and chief commissioner and directing them to arrest the accused. Sources in the police and Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) told Dawn that the prime minister called Inspector General Mohammad Sohail Chaudhry and Chief Commissioner Islamabad Sohail Ashraf and directed them to apprehend the man accused of defrauding the deceased student. The IG briefed the prime minister on the incident during the meeting. The capital police registered a case against the accused under Sections 322 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code on Saturday, following a complaint lodged by Mohammad Aijaz, a native of Sargodha residing in G-10. The accused allegedly defrauded the student of millions of rupees, following which she reportedly took her own life. Orders arrest of accused agent The minister of state for interior and narcotics control also contacted FIA officers and directed them to take strict action against the accused. The FIA Islamabad Zone has initiated an investigation and is conducting raids at various locations to trace and arrest him, according to a statement issued by the agency. The FIA Islamabad Zone director also visited Laiba’s residence, met her family and gathered details about the incident. According to the FIA, the accused allegedly gained the family’s trust by misrepresenting his identity and professional status before obtaining money from them for different purposes. He was not a registered visa agent but claimed to work as an accountant at the Supreme Court of Pakistan. He later made conflicting claims about his identity and employment, the agency said. The FIA statement said Rs550,000 was paid to the accused for securing employment for Laiba’s brother, while Rs7.2 million was handed over to him on the pretext of securing Laiba’s admission to Harvard University in the United States. The agency said the payments and claims made by the accused were being examined and further legal action would follow as the investigation progressed. Laiba had recently completed her BS degree from the International Islamic University Islamabad (IIUI). The accused allegedly defrauded her with the help of a female accomplice. According to a police report, her father contacted the police helpline after she went missing, saying she was under extreme psychological distress. Following an analysis of call detail records and location data, a joint police and family search found her body hanging by a scarf from a tree inside a fenced enclosure on the G-10 Sunday Bazaar green belt. The body was taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in an Edhi ambulance. After the autopsy, the victim’s clothes and biological samples were secured and sealed for forensic examination. The formal autopsy report is awaited. Investigators have secured the visa documents allegedly provided by the accused. A special police team has also been formed to trace and arrest him and his female accomplice. His name has been placed on the stop list to prevent him from leaving the country. Police sources said Laiba’s family had arranged money for the agent by selling a plot and gold ornaments. FO reiterates Pakistan's 'firm and unshakeable' commitment to Saudi Arabia's security after Riyadh attack. The Foreign Office (FO) on Sunday condemned a fresh wave of Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, reaffirming Pakistan’s “firm and unshakeable” commitment to the sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability of the Gulf state under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The defence pact , of which Turkiye is also a part, was signed on August 7 and aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. The statement comes following Saturday’s attack on Riyadh’s international airport, which killed at least 12 people and wounded 309 others. In a post on X, FO said the targeting of a civilian airport constituted “a heinous act of terrorism, a flagrant violation of international law and a grave threat to regional peace and security”. It expressed concern over the casualties resulting from the attack, extending condolences to the bereaved families and wishing a swift recovery to the injured. “The continued targeting of civilian population and critical infrastructure by the Houthi militia is utterly unacceptable and must be condemned unequivocally by the international community,” the statement read. It added: “Such brazen and indiscriminate acts of aggression cannot be justified under any circumstances and must cease immediately.” FO expressed “unwavering” solidarity with the leadership of Saudi Arabia and reiterated its “firm and unshakeable commitment” to Riyadh’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability in line with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the “recent decision” taken by its Strategic, Political and Defence Committee on October 5, in which the member states had agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in the kingdom. FO expressed support for Saudi Arabia’s right to self-defence against all threats and acts of aggression and went on to urge Yemen’s Houthis to cease attacks and the international community to take “a firm and unequivocal stand” against it. “Pakistan will continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, resolute in its commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and defence.” Shortly before FO, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, in a post on X, also condemned the attack. In his statement, the premier said that targeting civilian and critical infrastructure was “completely unacceptable and [constitutes] a serious threat to regional peace and stability. “Such acts of violence, which are a flagrant violation of international law, must cease immediately.” Expressing solidarity with Riyadh, PM Shehbaz said, “In accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the enduring bonds of brotherhood between our two countries, we reaffirm our steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.” The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has blamed the group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile. Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On Oct 5, in an emergency meeting of the Makkah pact in Riyadh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and was asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, to which he said both Turkiye and Pakistan had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

Indian court releases 'cockroach' movement leaders from detention. The founder of India’s youth-led online “cockroach” movement and two other leaders were released on Sunday, their lawyer said, a day after they were detained to thwart a major protest against the election commissioner. The group said thousands of protesters were detained before Saturday’s planned demonstration in New Delhi, the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision . Abhijeet Dipke and two other Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders were detained before they could disembark from their flight after arriving in the capital from Mumbai. Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post that Dipke and the others had been released by an executive magistrate’s court. She said they had been released on the condition that they made “no breach of peace for one year”. Dipke, wearing a white shirt, was driven away in a black vehicle soon after walking out of the court, AFP reporters saw. Authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital on Saturday, detaining thousands to prevent protesters from gathering at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar protest site, the CJP and Indian media reports said. The protest was organised to demand the resignation of the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI) over the nationwide voter-roll revision. Media reports said the revision resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists. Election authorities say the exercise was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. Critics say the process has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. The ECI has rejected allegations of wrongdoing. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) talk after their release at Delhi Cantt Police Station in New Delhi, India on October 11, 2026. —Reuters Saturday’s detentions triggered sharp criticism from opposition leaders, who accused Modi’s government of stifling dissent, and others. In Geneva, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in New Delhi. Both the CJP and opposition leader Rahul Gandhi have vowed to press ahead with protests despite the crackdown. Gandhi said his Congress party “and the youth of the country will once again take to the streets in large numbers” on Monday. “The more Modi and his government crack down, the more the anger of Gen Z and students will grow,” he said.

Broken record: The unfinished business of Partition. With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it. Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn , as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper. Though Dawn ’s archive goes back further, we have chosen to start from the day Pakistan was born. The news items have been selected for their relevance — in the eyes of this writer — to the modern day as well as their historical impact. ‘Friendship with Britain and Hindustan’ The front page of the Dawn Delhi edition of Aug 14, 1947 captured the zeitgeist of the time: a fond farewell to empire, and hope for the future. Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah, while delivering a speech at a state dinner in honour of Lord Louis Mountbatten, the last viceroy of India, spoke of the British warmly, saying Pakistan would “endeavour to create and maintain goodwill and friendship with Britain and our neighbouring dominion — Hindustan. …” Though relations with Britain saw ups and downs, they have remained generally cordial. The same, obviously, cannot be said for India. Mere months after the Quaid would express his desire for good relations with India, both nations went to war over Kashmir, as Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India, a process that would spark a dispute that remains unsolved to this day; despite how New Delhi may spin it, Jammu and Kashmir remains a disputed region. Moreover, Pakistan and India have fought numerous major and minor wars, with the last conflict breaking out in May 2025 after the Pahalgam incident. The unfinished business of Partition remains unfinished, and has resulted in a permanent state of hostility between Pakistan and India. A single-column news item on the front page reflected another, forgotten territorial dispute that has now become a part of history. It mentioned that the princely State of Junagadh, in the Kathiawar region of what is now India’s Gujarat state, had decided to join Pakistan. Mr. Ismail Abramani, Secretary for Constitutional Affairs to Junagadh State, “met Mr. Jinnah … and communicated to him the decision of the State.” Interestingly, when the Muslim nawab of Junagadh decided to accede to Pakistan, India did not accept it and occupied the state in November 1947. Yet the Kashmiri Hindu maharaja’s accession to India was perfectly acceptable to New Delhi. The Indian rulers of the time clearly shifted the goalposts when it suited them. Trouble in Lahore But with great hope there was also trepidation. The inside pages carried reports of communal disturbances which reflected the frenzy that accompanied Partition. A grim report from Lahore told the reader that “most of the sectors in the Walled City are on fire and burning unchecked”. It added that the military and police had been “firing incessantly in several places, where arson and looting was rampant”. So volatile was the situation that the district magistrate clamped an 11-hour curfew on many parts of the Punjab capital; three military brigades had to be moved in to control the situation. Disturbances had also been reported from Amritsar (East Punjab) and Moradabad (UP). Though Independence held great promise for the people of the subcontinent, freed as they were from colonial subjugation, as the record shows, the bitter rivalry between the erstwhile dominions of Pakistan and Hindustan has persisted, while communalism remains entrenched on both sides of the border. The pages of Dawn would over the decades tell these — and other — stories that shaped the future of Pakistan, and made it what it is today. It is these stories we will seek to examine every week.

Parliament’s place. MUCH has changed in just a little over a decade. In 2015, when the question of Pakistan’s involvement in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemeni rebels last arose, the then defence minister, Khawaja Asif, opened the issue for debate before a joint sitting of parliament. Days later, after a marathon session, it was the then finance minister, Ishaq Dar, who presented the parliamentary resolution affirming Pakistan’s support for Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, while conveying a desire to “maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”. In 2026, the Foreign Office tells us that the recent signing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the commitment of military capabilities under it are executive functions that do not necessarily require parliamentary approval. That is a rather large departure. Ironically, in his Friday briefing, the FO spokesperson, while rejecting criticism of the apparent lack of political consultation on the matter, pointed to the participation of Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in the Strategic Political and Defence Committee. He mentioned it in support of his assertion that members of parliament and the federal cabinet had not been completely cut off from the decision-making process. But the two ministers ought to be asked: is the risk calculus of the conflict any different from before? And if the policy is the same as in 2015, why not say so in parliament, as they did then? One hopes they have satisfactory answers to these questions. The secrecy surrounding the matter gives the impression that, in 2026, parliament is being deliberately sidelined in a matter in which it was deliberately involved in 2015. Meanwhile, the third party in the trilateral Makkah defence agreement, Turkiye , is taking the agreement to its parliament. Regardless of what the law allows, it would be better if Pakistan took the same route. The fact that our troops are already on Saudi soil, and have been so for decades, is no answer, especially since the terms of the new joint defence agreement have not been made public, and, therefore, their consequences cannot be judged. A handful of ministers in a committee deliberating behind closed doors cannot be claimed as a substitute for a parliamentary debate. Where Pakistan’s involvement in a foreign conflict is concerned, the public’s representatives should have been taken into confidence. Pakistan has always been unequivocal about its commitment to protect Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and the holy sites — that is not in question here. The concern is about process, and respect for parliament as the people’s representative. Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

Experiment or stick with the winning XI? Pakistan face selection dilemma ahead of second Sri Lanka T20I. Pakistan will meet Sri Lanka on Sunday evening for the second of a three-match Twenty20 international series, where the Green Shirts will look to take an unassailable 2-0 lead and seal the series. Pakistan’s standout performers, Maaz Sadaqat and skipper Sahibzada Farhan will look to replicate their respective strong outings from Friday, with both declaring their commitment to playing their natural game in a way that the modern format demands. In the post-match press conference after the first match on Friday, top-order batter Maaz said that he planned on backing his natural game and play the way he has been playing, Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by four wickets, accomplished with a largely untroubled chase of the 183-run target which they achieved with seven balls remaining, despite a cluster of wickets falling at the toe-end of the innings. “It was my first 50 so I am very happy,” said Maaz, who scored a maiden, blistering T20 international half-century off 26 balls at one-drop. “The plan for upcoming matches is to play the way I have been playing and back it.” Maaz’s rich vein of form can be traced back to last month’s Caribbean Premiere League (CPL), where he scored 363 runs in seven matches at a strike rate of almost 175. His campaign also included two centuries, one of which came in the competition’s final. In the second match of the series, Maaz can potentially cement his spot in the side further. It could also be interesting to note whether Maaz remains at one-drop, or if Pakistan want to test him as an opener. Maaz himself believes the two positions are interchangeable, which he said whilst answering a question about whether taking over the position Babar Azam normally played in was a source of extra pressure. “I am comfortable in this position, but for Pakistan I am prepared to bat at any position,” he said. Farhan, too, backed Maaz. “I think, the sort of form Maaz is in, he is one of the best players,” he said after the first match. “I told him to take advantage of his current form,” he said, adding that he was “very happy” as his captain. “Today I told him, now that you have the opportunity, you should complete your 50. If you complete your 5o, we can finish this match three or four overs earlier,” Farhan later told the broadcaster in the post-match show. The skipper was named player of the match himself for his 53-ball-89, in his third match as T20I captain following the two matches that were part of the team’s silver-winning Asian Games campaign. He added that he had changed the way he played over the last year to strike at at least 150-160 instead of the lower strike rates he used to record before, because such is the demand of the modern game. Echoing Maaz’s sentiment, he added that he will continue to bat the way he has been batting and not change it as long as the game demanded it, “whether I am captain or not.” The series is his first assignment at home as captain, and its outcome and findings could be formative for a Pakistan T20 side that is somewhat in the process of a re-build, with senior mainstays like Babar Azam, Mohammad Rizwan and Shaheen Afridi not currently part of the squad. It provides an opportunity for the management and the new skipper to further assess team combinations and line-ups. “It would be a lie to say there is no pressure, because when you are representing your country, people have expectations from you,” the captain said. ‘‘As a captain, I am very happy with this team… (In T20s) I think three or four boys perform and it is enough to turn the tables in a match.” “If you look at it, we have Arafat Minhas as a backup. We have Abdul Samad, Sufiyan Muqeem. So, our back-up strength is very strong,” he said, adding that this bench strength also meant that the playing combinations were not fixed and that they could always experiment and change in upcoming matches. Whether Pakistan chooses to actually test the strength of its bench could be another interesting element to look out for, going into this second match. All of them have made a case for themselves: Arafat bowled a disciplined spell of 2-23 in three overs in the Asian Games semi-final. And though not in the same format, he has already starred in the greens, picking up a Player of the Series award in his debut One-day International series against Australia earlier this year. Abdul Samad’s clinical 15-ball-30 against Bangladesh played a starring role in the team reaching the gold-medal match in the Asian Games. And while Sufiyan’s returns against India were not entirely prodigal, he is still coming off the back of a T20 season that saw him named Player of the Tournament in Peshawar Zalmi’s Pakistan Super League title-winning run and, more recently, be named Player of the Final in the CPL for a record spell of 4-14. Pakistan’s previous T20 sides were often criticised for not using bilateral fixtures to amply experiment and give match time to young players, focusing too much on the results as opposed to the long-term process. Maaz, for example, was asked in the press conference whether Shadab Khan was occupying a space that could potentially have gone to a younger player (to which his response was simple: “He was selected on merit.”) Whether Pakistan seek to play a fresher XI tonight, or chooses to not fix what was not broken in the first match, remains to be seen.

Governor’s rule and emergency imposed in KP — here’s what it means. The federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa amid growing tensions with the PTI-led provincial government, including disagreements over counterterrorism policy amid a deteriorating security situation in the province. The decision was taken under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan. Here is what it means. Governor’s rule Article 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan stipulates that, if the president believes that a provincial government cannot function in accordance with the Constitution, the federal government can assume control of the province. This can be done either directly or by assigning the relevant functions to the provincial governor — hence the term governor’s rule. Under this arrangement, the powers of the provincial assembly can be exercised by Parliament. However, neither the president nor the governor can assume the powers of the high court or suspend its operations. Moreover, governor’s rule can be imposed for an initial period of two months, with a joint sitting of Parliament able to approve an extension of up to two months at a time. In total, governor’s rule can remain in place for a maximum of six months. State of emergency Meanwhile, under Article 232, which pertains to the proclamation of an emergency, the provincial assembly continues to function as usual. However, if a provincial law conflicts with a federal law enacted by Parliament, the latter takes precedence. Lawyer Basil Nabi Malik, speaking to Dawn , explained that the chief minister would remain in office during a state of emergency. However, the federal government could assume certain functions of the provincial government. An emergency also allows the federal government to make provisions it considers necessary and suspend certain constitutional provisions relating to provincial bodies. However, as with governor’s rule, the federal government cannot assume the powers of a high court. It also empowers Parliament to confer powers and impose duties on federal government officers in the province. It further stipulates that laws passed by Parliament solely on account of the emergency will cease to have effect six months after the emergency ends. The proclamation of emergency lapses after two months unless it is approved by a resolution of a joint sitting of Parliament.

Emergency provisions. This opinion piece was originally published on Dec 25, 2022. WITH each passing day, the state of animosity between the PTI, along with the two provincial governments it controls, and the federal government, that is composed of a multiparty coalition, is getting more intense. Both parties are trying all weapons available in the constitutional armoury. Constitutional provisions are, at times, stretched to the limit — and even beyond — but when the courts adjudicate disputes, despite the disapproval of and grumbling by the losing party, the verdict is generally respected and enforced. No-confidence resolutions have been tabled and, in the case of the National Assembly, passed too, culminating in the exit of prime minister Imran Khan . The Punjab chief minister has been asked by the governor to prove that he still commands a majority in the provincial assembly. In the escalating confrontation, at least two senior leaders have alluded to the possibility of using the ultimate weapon of emergency provisions. The Punjab chief minister had referred to ‘financial emergency’ after his short trip to Rawalpindi recently and earlier Interior Minister Rana Sanaullah had hinted at moving a summary for ‘governor’s rule’ in Punjab when the PTI spokesperson Fawad Chaudhry had mentioned the possibility of arresting him in the province. There is no doubt that emergency provisions are very much a part of the Constitution, but their use usually indicates a shattered polity and a part of the provisions dealing with ‘financial emergency’ may deliver a deathblow to an already fragile economy. These provisions, therefore, better be left unused. Since provincial governors generally assume executive power of a province during an emergency, it is also referred to as ‘governor’s rule’. There is no doubt that emergency provisions are a part of the Constitution, but their use indicates a shattered polity. Part 10 of the Constitution covers emergency provisions and comprises six articles — Article 232 to Article 237. Three of these articles are of prime importance. It is usually a province which bears the brunt of an emergency proclamation. This is why these provisions have assumed importance during this time of confrontation between the federal government and the Punjab provincial government. Article 232 deals with the emergency, which is pronounced in two distinct situations. One, war or external aggression and, two, internal disturbances beyond the power of a province to control. If an emergency is to be pronounced because of internal security conditions of a province, then the provincial assembly concerned is required to pass a resolution. The president can also proclaim an emergency, but in this case the proclamation would need to be placed before parliament, whose two Houses should approve it within 10 days. During the emergency under this article, the provincial assembly can continue to work, but a law passed by parliament for the province will have precedence over provincial laws. The executive authority of the federal government extends to the province which will be exercised either by the president or the provincial governor. The powers of the courts will, however, remain unchanged during the emergency. The proclamation of an emergency needs to be placed before a joint sitting of parliament within 30 days of the proclamation. Its validity is for two months, unless the joint sitting approves an extension through a resolution. If the joint sitting disapproves the proclamation, it will cease to be in force. An important aspect of the emergency under this article is that parliament, during the emergency, may extend the term of the National Assembly for a period of up to one year, but this extra term cannot extend beyond six months after the proclamation ceases to be in force. Article 233 explains that the president will have the power to suspend certain fundamental rights under the emergency proclamation. Article 234 deals with the power to impose emergency in case of failure of the constitutional machinery in a province. This probably is the article which provinces should be most concerned about. The imposition of this emergency may happen after the president receives a report from the provincial governor and the president is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the provincial government cannot carry out its duties out in accordance with the Constitution. In case the two Houses of parliament pass a resolution separately demanding that such an emergency be imposed, the president is bound to proclaim the emergency. The powers of the courts, however, will remain intact even during the emergency. A proclamation issued under Article 234 has to be laid before a joint sitting of parliament and is valid only for two months, unless the joint sitting extends the validity for a further period of two months. The maximum validity of such a proclamation is six months. The proclamation under this article may declare that the powers of the provincial assembly are exercisable by or under the authority of parliament. The joint sitting of parliament can also confer power on the president to make laws for the provincial assembly. The president, when parliament is not in session, may also authorise expenditure from the provincial consolidated fund to be later sanctioned by a joint sitting of parliament. Article 235 deals with proclamation of a financial emergency by the president if he is satisfied after consultation with the governor or governors that a situation has arisen whereby economic life, financial stability or the credit of Pakistan or any part of it is threatened. While such proclamation of emergency is in force, the executive authority of the federation extends to giving directions to any province to observe such principles of financial propriety as may be specified in the directions. These directions may include reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of a province or the federation. This proclamation is also required to be laid before a joint sitting of parliament and may be extended up to six months as in the case of proclamation under Article 234. The writer is president of the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development And Transparency. president@pildat.org Twitter: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, December 25th, 2022

Soldier martyred, 12 terrorists killed as security forces foil infiltration attempt in Kurram: ISPR. A soldier was martyred and 12 terrorists killed in an exchange of fire in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kurram district, the army’s media wing said on Sunday. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said that the movement of a group of khawarij attempting to cross the international border from Afghanistan into Pakistan was detected in Kurram district on Sunday, where security forces engaged them effectively. Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. Security forces, “maintaining a high state of alertness and vigilance, effectively thwarted the infiltration attempt”, the statement added. It further said that Afghan Taliban posts had also opened fire to support the infiltration attempt by the khawarij. “The skilful and precise engagement by vigilant troops resulted in the killing of 12 khawarij and Afghan Taliban,” the statement said. During the exchange of fire, Naib Subedar Hidayat Aman was martyred after “fighting gallantly”. This incident along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border vindicates Islamabad’s “objective and factual stance regarding the willful abject failure of the Afghan Taliban regime to deny the use of Afghan soil to the terrorist organisation”, the statement added. “The security forces of Pakistan remain resolute and unwavering in their commitment to defend the nation’s frontiers,” said the ISPR, adding that sanitisation operation is being conducted in the area to eliminate any other Indian sponsored khawariji found in the area.” “The relentless counter-terrorism campaign under vision Azm-i-Istehkam as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign sponsored and supported terrorism from the country.” “These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation and its frontiers at all costs,” it said. In a statement on X, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the security forces for “foiling the infiltration attempt”. He expressed “heartfelt condolences and expression of sympathy” to the bereaved family of the martyred Naib Subedar Hidayat Aman, adding that nation takes pride in the “professional capabilities and courage” of the security forces. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time September particularly witnessed a significant deterioration in Pakistan’s overall security environment, accompanied by growing political, economic and regional pressures, according to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS) . Terrorist violence increased substantially , with 225 attacks recorded nationwide, compared with 199 in August, representing a 13.1 per cent increase and the highest monthly total recorded in 12 years. On Sept 27 , 14 people, including two rescue officials, were martyred and 35 sustained injuries after a suicide bomber rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into a police checkpost in and then targeted an ambulance taking bodies to hospital in DI Khan. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation .

Timeline: A concise history of emergency rule in Pakistan. The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule. Article 232 of the Constitution deals with “proclamation of emergency on account of war and internal disturbance”, while Article 234 of the Constitution, more commonly known as “governor’s rule”, empowers the federal government to take control of a province in case of “failure of constitutional machinery”. This isn’t the first time the Centre has used its powers to declare emergency in a province or even send the respective provincial government packing. Here’s a brief history of emergency rule in Pakistan. January 1949 to April 1951 The first governor’s rule was imposed within a short span of the country’s establishment, in the heartland of Punjab. In January 1949, then Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan visited Lahore, where Chief Minister Nawab Mamdot told him that he had earned the confidence of a majority of the MPAs in the provincial assembly. The development had come about due to a disagreement between Mamdot and former CM Mumtaz Daulatana. However, Liaquat Ali Khan noted factual discrepancies in the document shown by Mamdot. He dismissed the Mamdot government, dissolved the assembly, and imposed governor’s rule in the province. December 1951 to May 1953 — Sindh A governor’s rule of 1 year and 144 days lasted in Sindh after Chief Minister Muhammad Ayub Khuhro was dismissed amid allegations of corruption and maladministration. Mian Aminuddin administered the province directly under Governor’s rule, which ended following the 1953 provincial elections, after which Pirzada Abdus Sattar of the Pakistan Muslim League took over. February-April, 1973 — Balochistan On February 14, 1973, Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto dismissed the Balochistan provincial government led by Chief Minister Sardar Attaullah Mengal and removed Governor Mir Ghaus Bakhsh Bizenjo, citing alleged involvement in unrest and the discovery of weapons at the Iraqi embassy in Islamabad. The next day, Nawab Akbar Khan Bugti was appointed as the new Governor of Balochistan, and direct central/governor’s rule was enforced. The federal government also subsequently deployed the Pakistan Army under General Tikka Khan to conduct operations in the mountainous and tribal regions, particularly targeting areas like Lasbela and Marri. The governor’s rule ended in late April the same year, paving the way for Jam Ghulam Qadir Khan to form a new provincial ministry. February-May 1975 — Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor’s rule was imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (then known as the North-West Frontier Province) from February 16, 1975, to May 3, 1975, for a total duration of 76 days under Article 232 of the 1973 Constitution due to an emergency. Officials had cited external disruptions beyond local control. At the time, the federal government under PM Bhutto had directed the governor to assume all government powers, ending the cabinet of Chief Minister Sardar Inayatullah Khan Gandapur. The province was overseen by Major General (R) Syed Ghawas until direct rule concluded on May 3, 1975, with Nasrullah Khan Khattak assuming the office of Chief Minister. June-August 1988 — Sindh The second instance of a governor’s rule in Sindh’s history lasted 68 days, from June 24, 1988, to August 31, 1988. The caretaker government of Chief Minister Akhtar Ali Ghulam Qazi of the Islami Jamhoori Ittehad was dismissed. Qazi was replaced by Pakistan Army’s four-star general Rahimuddin Khan as governor. This development came closely after President General Zia-ul-Haq’s nationwide dissolution of Prime Minister Mohammad Khan Junejo’s federal government and all provincial assemblies on May 29, 1988. February-April 1994 — Khyber Pakhtunkhwa One of the country’s most controversial political episodes, the governor’s rule imposed in KP from February 25, 1994 to April 24, 1994 came after Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto suspended the PML-N ministry in the province, led by Sabir Shah. Executive authority was temporarily transferred directly to the provincial Governor, Major General (Retd) Khurshid Ali Khan. When the governor’s rule was lifted, Aftab Ahmad Khan Sherpao of the PPP was sworn in as the new chief minister of the province February-March 2009 — Punjab President Asif Ali Zardari imposed governor’s rule for two months, dismissing PML-N’s government after the Supreme Court disqualified Nawaz Sharif and Shehbaz Sharif. Zardari appointed Salman Taseer as the governor of Punjab. The provincial assembly was not suspended, but then-CM Shehbaz and his cabinet members were barred from holding office. The governor’s rule was lifted after a month. January-March 2013 — Balochistan PPP’s Prime Minister Raja Pervez Ashraf dismissed Balochistan’s provincial government, yielding to nationwide protests. His announcement came as thousands of Hazara Shias staged a sit-in in freezing cold on Alamdar Road for three days, along with the bodies of dozens of people killed in twin bombings in Quetta The carnage had resulted in over 90 fatalities. The provincial government of Chief Minister Nawab Aslam Raisani was sacked, and Governor Nawab Zulfiqar Ali Magsi took charge as the chief executive of the province. Nationwide emergencies Nationwide emergencies have been imposed several times as well, including martial laws, with the first one just a few years after Pakistan’s creation, in 1954. Intercity transport suspended in Lahore, bus terminals reportedly sealed. LAHORE: Intercity bus services from Lahore to several destinations across the country were suspended on Sunday after the administration reportedly sealed all general bus terminals in the city late on Saturday night, leaving passengers stranded and disrupting travel. The closures affected passengers travelling to Islamabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, southern Punjab and other parts of central Punjab. Several passengers reported difficulties after their tickets were cancelled and transport services suspended. Meanwhile, major private bus operators, including Faisal Movers and Daewoo, suspended their services amid reports of restrictions on public transport movement on motorways and national highways. Representatives of Faisal Movers and Daewoo told Dawn that their services had been suspended and buses were not being dispatched due to the restrictions. However, motorway police spokesperson Imran Shah told Dawn that motorways and highways were open to traffic and that he was unaware of any directions to suspend bus services. Another motorway police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said buses were not operating on motorways or highways because of the PTI’s protest call. He added that people travelling in private vehicles could use the roads. Punjab Transport Department Secretary Imran Sikandar Baloch was unavailable for comment despite repeated attempts to contact him on his mobile phone. The development comes as the PTI launched its march on October 4 despite warnings from the Centre. So far, the march — being carried out to demand Imran’s release — has remained within KP, where the PTI is in power. A day earlier, containers were transported to Swabi Interchange — where the PTI had called on its workers to gather — as well as the Indus River bridge on the M-1 Motorway to block the party’s march, but the motorway and the Grand Trunk Road remain open to traffic.

'No lesson learnt': KP emergency evokes grim October memories. Sunday, Oct 11, evoked grim memories for many in Pakistan, as the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The cabinet was certain of the decision, but many others warned against repeating what they saw as an “ill-advised step”. Nevertheless, it happened, again. The threat of emergency and governor’s rule had been looming over the province for days, after the PTI announced its long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. It materialised on Sunday. It began with a federal cabinet meeting where Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was briefed on the security situation in KP, which the Centre had earlier been linking with the need for emergency in the province. The cabinet reviewed the situation, took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”, and gave the nod to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP. A signature by President Asif Ali Zardari, and the decision was implemented shortly after. The development took veteran journalist Mazhar Abbas on a trip down memory lane, apparently a grim one. “Why [does] October often bring ‘bad news’ for democracy from 1958 to 2026?” he posted on X. “Saddest part is that each time one party or the other welcomed such moves. On Oct 12, 1999 when PM Nawaz was sacked, the PPP welcomed the move. Now, the PPP and PML-N agreed to get rid of the PTI KP government. No lesson learnt,” he lamented. Former ambassador and analyst Maleeha Lodhi agreed. “Really nothing learnt from history,” she too posted, replying to Abbas’s comment. Analyst Niaz Murtaza was more thorough in recounting the historical trend of what Abbas described as “bad news” from October. “October is perhaps the worst month for democracy,” Murtaza commented, sharing a list of instances from history: On the latest imposition of emergency in KP, he said the move was “deeply condemnable, unfortunate and ill-advised”. “The clearly illegitimate nature of the central government makes it doubly so. This could make the situation in KP much more complicated,” he warned. Others, too, warned against the move and its consequences. Among them was National Democratic Movement Chairperson Bushra Gohar, who posted a warning the night before emergency was imposed. “Emergency will further aggravate the already volatile political and security situation in Pakhtunkhwa. The province cannot afford yet another failed experiment after the disastrous pro-Taliban TTPTI government — 13 years of incompetence, loot and plunder, death and devastation,” she posted on X on the night before emergency was imposed. Instead, she added, free, fair and credible elections were the only way forward. Similarly, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan cautioned the federal government and Parliament in a statement that declaring emergency or imposing governor’s rule in KP risked further deepening of political tensions and undermining of democratic processes. “We strongly urge the federal government and the PTI to resume a meaningful political dialogue immediately and ensure that citizens’ fundamental rights are not suspended under any pretext,” the statement said. Lawyer Rida Hosain pointed to the potential implication of emergency particularly for former tribal areas. She noted in a post on X that the imposition of emergency allowed the executive to suspend certain fundamental rights. “To impose emergency rule over the former tribal areas is to push the people of those areas back into a legal black hole where their fundamental rights are treated as dispensable,” she said. Journalist Ihsanullah Tipu Mehsud saw emergency as a move that “frees the PTI” and “traps the Centre”. Because “Islamabad owns security, PTI owns the narrative,” he explained on X. Former IT minister Umar Saif explained Mehsud’s deduction in more detail, saying that imposing emergency in KP “comes with an enormous burden of responsibility”. “It is not merely an exercise of authority; it is a commitment to fix what has gone wrong. The government must now deliver. Failure will deepen public disillusionment, hand fresh ammunition to the naysayers, and discredit the very idea of reform. “Reform demands clarity of intent, consistency of purpose, and the resolve to see it through. We have seen too many initiatives falter midway, leaving behind resentment and eroding faith in the process,” he said. Meanwhile, journalist Shahzad Iqbal noted that PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had called emergency a “political atomic bomb”. “Yet President Zardari has completed hat-trick of imposing governor’s rule,” he said, recounting the previous two instances — in 2009 in Punjab and in 2013 in Balochistan. “The irony is hard to miss,” he commented.
