Sri Lanka win toss, opt to bowl first in second T20I against Pakistan. Pakistan will look to seal the series after a comprehensive four-wicket victory on the back of skipper Sahibzada Farhan’s scintillating 89 and Maaz Sadaqat’s maiden half century in the first T20I. In the post-match press conference after the match, top-order batter Maaz said that he planned on backing his natural game and play the way he has been playing, Pakistan accomplished the 183-run target largely untroubled, achieving it seven balls to spare, despite a cluster of wickets falling at the toe-end of the innings. “It was my first 50 so I am very happy,” said Maaz, who scored a maiden, blistering T20 international half-century off 26 balls at one-drop. “The plan for upcoming matches is to play the way I have been playing and back it.” The series Farhan’s first assignment at home as captain, and its outcome and findings could be formative for a Pakistan T20 side that is somewhat in the process of a re-build, with senior mainstays like Babar Azam, Mohammad Rizwan and Shaheen Afridi not currently part of the squad. It provides an opportunity for the management and the new skipper to further assess team combinations and line-ups. “It would be a lie to say there is no pressure, because when you are representing your country, people have expectations from you,” the captain said. ‘‘As a captain, I am very happy with this team… (In T20s) I think three or four boys perform and it is enough to turn the tables in a match.” Teams: PAKISTAN: Sahibzada Farhan (captain), Fakhar Zaman, Maaz Sadaqat, Hasan Nawaz, Saim Ayub, Khawaja Nafay (wicket-keeper), Shadab Khan, Mohammad Imran, Salman Mirza, Naseem Shah, Abrar Ahmed SRI LANKA: Lahiru Udara, Sineth Jayasuriya, Kusal Mendis (captain and wicket-keeper), Kamindu Mendis, Sahan Arachchige, Dasun Shanaka, Chamindu Wickramasinghe, Maheesh Theekshana, Eshan Malinga, Binura Fernando, Nuwan Thushara

Containers placed in Peshawar after federal govt imposes emergency in KP. PESHAWAR: Shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block roads after the federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday. The measures, imposed earlier, have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, according to a statement by the President House. They were imposed following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. Containers were placed near Peshawar’s railway station to block the routes towards Khyber Bazaar, Shoba Bazaar and beyond. They were also placed near Edwardes College to block entry to Jail Road and Malik Saad Shaheed Flyover. Additionally, containers near Bala Hisar Fort and outside the Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) office blocked entry towards Mall Road. Police were reportedly deployed in significant numbers, particularly around Governor House. The deployment included personnel called from other districts. The military has been deployed only at check posts, as is routine. Only official vehicles are being allowed to travel from Governor House towards the Chief Minister’s House. Royal Artillery (RA) Bazaar has been closed, while Saddar remains partially open. Earlier, traffic jams were reported due to the closure of the main Khyber Road, which connects the city’s Grand Trunk (GT) Road with the eastern side of University Road and serves as the main artery and choke point. The resulting diversions created pressure on auxiliary roads. The area is part of the cantonment, and the Red Zone contains important installations such as the Corps Commander’s House, civil secretariat, central police office, CM Secretariat, CM House and Governor House. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. On Saturday, KP Inspector General of Police (IGP) Zulfiqar Hameed put district police on alert for possible violent protests and sabotage in the event of an emergency in the province, emphasising caution in the use of force. A notification issued by the IGP’s office said district police officers (DPOs) could issue appropriate directions, instructions or guidelines to regulate protests and ensure public safety. In the event of violence, they could also take necessary legal action. KP House sealed, NPC refuses to allow TTAP presser In Islamabad, the main opposition alliance — which would typically hold pressers at KP House — could not find a place to hold a press conference in the urban areas as KP House was sealed. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) has therefore decided to hold its presser at Jamia Al Wilaya near Bhara Kahu on the Murree Expressway. Speaking to Dawn , TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai said that after deciding to hold a press conference, the alliance initially thought to go to KP House, but came to know that it had been sealed. He added that they then decided to hold it at the National Press Club (NPC), but were refused by the club despite being willing to pay the fee. “Now we have decided to hold the presser at Bhara Kahu,” he said.

Emergency, governor's rule imposed in KP as president approves cabinet decision. Key developments: Emergency imposed under Article 232 , governor’s rule under Article 234 Cabinet recommended move due to KP govt’s ‘deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam appointed as KP chief secretary PTI’s Gohar condemns decision as undemocratic, says peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy Governor Kundi calls for unity for ‘new chapter’ in KP’s development ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule. Following the imposition, internet disruptions were being reported from parts of Peshawar, with Dawn unable to contact its correspondents there. Earlier in the day, massive police deployment and increased barriers on certain routes using containers were witnessed in the city. According to sources in the telecom sector, mobile network and data services have been slowed or shut down in selected areas of some cities. However, there is no province-wide shutdown of mobile data or internet. The decision to impose the provisions came during an emergency meeting of the federal cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, where he was briefed on the security situation in KP. A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. The members proposed, given the “gravity” of the situation, that the PM advise the president to exercise “his constitutional authority and impose an emergency in the province under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution”. A couple of hours after the decision was announced, KP Information Minister Shafi Jan, who had been accompanying Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on the PTI’s long march , claimed that the KP CM had been taken into custody. Dawn has reached out to police for a comment. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. It may be recalled that in July 2024, when Afridi’s predecessor Ali Amin Gandapur was the chief minister, the KP Assembly passed a resolution urging the federal government to consult with it and the provincial government before launching a new military operation. The resolution, passed by a majority vote, cautioned that proceeding without provincial consent could hinder the offensive’s success and result in adverse consequences, for which the federal government would be responsible. In December that year, the assembly voted unanimously against a potential military operation in parts of Khyber and Bannu districts. About a year later, after Afridi became the KP CM, the provincial assembly convened a grand jirga with Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and other parties in attendance. The moot unanimously demanded that the Centre prioritise negotiations with Afghanistan and consult the KP government over Afghan policy. Constitutional provisions Emergency Article 232 of the Constitution provides for the proclamation of emergency in a province. It says, “If the president is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency.” However, invoking this article “due to internal disturbances beyond the powers of a provincial government to control” requires a resolution from the provincial assembly of that province. In case the president “acts on his own” — which is not currently the case — the Proclamation of Emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days. According to this provision, parliament “shall have power to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during the time of the proclamation of an emergency. Nothing in this Article shall restrict the power of a provincial assembly to make any law which the Constitution empowers it to make, but if any provision of a provincial law is repugnant to any provision of an Act by Parliament, the latter would prevail and the provincial law would be void as long as the parliamentary Act is in effect. Governor’s rule On the other hand, Article 234 deals with the imposition of the governor’s rule “in case of failure of constitutional machinery in a province”. For imposition of the governor’s rule, the president simply requires a request from the provincial governor, it says. “A proclamation issued under this Article shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolution of the joint sitting and may by like resolution be extended for a further period not exceeding two months at a time,” the Constitution reads. However, it adds that no such proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than six months. Article 233, which provides powers to the president to suspend certain fundamental rights during the emergency period, was not mentioned in the summary signed by President Zardari. Chief secretary appointed Following the approval, the federal government appointed Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan as the chief secretary of KP, according to an official notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn. The appointment will take effect immediately and remain in place until further orders, it said. Dr Irfan, a Grade 22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), was previously serving as secretary of the Power Division in the federal Ministry of Energy. He hails from Mardan. In a separate notification, the federal government also placed Muhammad Yahya Akhunzada at the disposal of the KP government with “immediate effect and until further orders”. Akhunzada, a Grade 20 PAS officer, was serving as an additional secretary at PMO. He hails from Charsadda and has also served as additional political agent for North and South Waziristan, secretary of health, information and education in KP, and commissioner of Dera Ismail Khan. ‘Peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy’ PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan strongly condemned the imposition of emergency in KP and “completely rejected” it. “This is an extremely alarming and grave political mistake and an undemocratic measure — the people will never accept such actions against their rights,” Gohar wrote in a post on X. He stated: “There is still time; this decision can be withdrawn in a few days. Let the federation set aside its ego, understand the ground realities, accept legitimate demands, respect the sentiments and emotions of the people, and save the country from further political and economic damage and from pushing back the democratic process. “Revisiting political decisions is not a sign of weakness but of wisdom in the national interest — otherwise, great damage will be done.” Stressing that the mandate of the people of KP was their constitutional and legal right, the PTI chairman said: “Peace cannot be established, nor stability brought, by ignoring this mandate, weakening provincial autonomy, and creating conflict between the federation and the province.” He asserted that there was “no disagreement on eliminating terrorism, but the fight against terrorism cannot be used as a justification to suppress the people’s voice, achieve political objectives, or limit the province’s constitutional authority”. “Terrorism can only be combated through national unity and a joint strategy,” Gohar maintained. “The federation cannot be strengthened by weakening the provinces. The solution to problems lies not in force, confrontation, and extraordinary measures, but in political wisdom, supremacy of the Constitution, and meaningful negotiations and practical steps.” The PTI chairman said his party will raise the matter on “every constitutional, legal, and democratic forum for the protection of the people’s mandate, provincial autonomy, and constitutional and democratic rights”. PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram told Dawn that the party has called a meeting of the parliamentary committee to mull three options as a counterstrategy. “We will discuss challenging the decision in the court, boycotting the National Assembly, Senate and proceedings in provincial assemblies,” he said. Peaceful protests across the country were also under consideration. However, he said that the final decision will be taken by the PTI’s political committee. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), of which PTI is a part, termed the move a violation of the Constitution. In a statement, the opposition alliance particularly assailed President Zardari’s PPP, claiming that the “most undemocratic actions and the imposition of governor’s rule” had been the hallmark of the party in the country’s history. “On the one hand, despite the extremely dire administrative and law and order situation in Balochistan, no such step has been taken, while on the other hand, this province — whose assembly and government stand on the true and real mandate of the people — has been targeted,” it contended. TTAP said it would convene a meeting on the matter and announce a joint course of action. Separately, the PTI parliamentary committee held a meeting and categorically rejected the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. In a statement, it termed the development “a direct assault on the public mandate and an unacceptable move”. “In a three-hour-long meeting of the PTI parliamentary party, the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was strongly condemned and unanimously rejected. The meeting declared this step contrary to facts, unconstitutional, undemocratic, and a blatant insult to the public mandate of the province,” the statement said. “The parliamentary party made it clear that measures to render the elected provincial government ineffective and usurp its constitutional powers could pose grave threats to the federal system and democratic traditions. Such decisions will increase political instability and public unrest in the province, while already existing tensions between the federation and the province will further intensify,” it added. The statement added that the solution to political differences should be found through constitutional and democratic procedures and mutual consultation, rather than through force and coercion. It also raised serious questions regarding the conduct of the federal government. “The parliamentary party took the stance that if terrorism and the deteriorating law and order situation are the primary justification for the imposition of emergency, then why is the situation in Balochistan being ignored?” the statement asked. The meeting also made it clear that Afridi was the elected chief minister a member of the provincial assembly. “Measures regarding his arrest, detention, or the usurping of his constitutional and democratic powers were strongly condemned. The meeting termed such actions an insult to the public mandate and a dangerous precedent for democratic traditions,” it said. Governor Kundi urges unity for ‘new chapter’ Meanwhile, Governor Kundi said the decision was made for “establishing peace in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the prosperity of its people, and the development of the province”. “I am your governor, but beyond that, I want to play my role as a servant of this soil and a protector of your rights. Let us come together to bring peace to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and begin a new chapter of our province’s development,” he said in a statement. Kundi assured the public that it was his responsibility to raise their issues on the relevant forums. Recalling the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism, he said, “Now the time has come that we do not let these sacrifices go to waste and together establish lasting peace in our province.” The PPP leader urged the public to set aside their political differences and unite for the province’s peace, the protection of its people, and the future of the coming generations. “We must not let our differences become an obstacle in the path of our province’s common interests.” Cannot allow PTI to destabilise the economy: PM tells cabinet Addressing the cabinet meeting, the premier said the PTI-led KP government cannot be allowed to derail the stabilising economy amid tensions between the two sides. “I will not allow them (PTI) to destabilise the economy,” he said during the meeting. On terrorism in KP and Balochistan, the premier said, “The way common citizens are being martyred, the way police officials and security officials, children and mothers [..] there can be nothing more heart-wrenching.” He recalled that Pakistan has repeatedly urged neighbouring Afghanistan to rein in the terrorist elements; however, “they still do not understand it”. PM Shehbaz also reiterated his condemnation of the recent deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, noting the long-standing fraternal ties between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. “Our only goal is that peace should be restored in the region,” he said. “Pakistan expresses solidarity with Saudi Arabia and stands with it. We will not tolerate any aggression against Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that it was a “red line” for Pakistan. During his address, PM Shehbaz also spoke of the recent staff-level agreement reached with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). “It is hoped that we will unlock the $1.2 billion tranche within this year,” he said, recalling a meeting with the IMF’s Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last month. He commended the political and military leadership for “working together day and night” in bringing fiscal discipline to Pakistan. The premier recalled his visit to London last month, where he had met with senior executives from leading global financial institutions. He also spoke of Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the international community, taking note of the appreciation Pakistan has received for mediation in the Middle East conflict. “Pakistan continues to play its role with hard work and sincerity,” he said, particularly lauding the role of the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 12; Saudi-led coalition vows 'decisive' response to worst attack on kingdom in a decade. At least 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in an attack on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, as the Houthis escalate a campaign they launched this summer. The dead from the third attack this week on the airport included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, 309 were wounded, officials said. While the Houthis stopped short of claiming the strike, they threatened new attacks on the kingdom’s airports, except for the holy cities of Makkah and Madina, warning passengers not to travel. “The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces,” military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X. President Donald Trump said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, some in critical condition after the attack, which occurred without warning. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the Houthi attack on Sunday, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile. Earlier in the day, authorities had suspended operations at Riyadh’s international airport. The Saudi civil aviation authority had initially confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the “serious emergency”, a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday. Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said 155 arriving and 161 departing flights had been cancelled, while a total of 222 flights were delayed. At around 6pm local time, Flightradar24 noted that flights bound for the airport were “diverting elsewhere, mainly to Jeddah at the moment”. It later shared a notice to airmen (Notam) for operations suspended till 12am. A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic. “I was on gate 403” at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP . “I saw 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.” A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday. “We were told we are dealing with a ‘serious emergency situation’. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh”, with many in critical condition, the source said. The aviation authority said the number of injured from the attack was still being assessed, adding that airport “operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities”. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with “dozens of people injured” in all. A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass. Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport. Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Makkah had been injured while waiting to board their flight. A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by “a missile around 3:00pm” (5pm PKT). “Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target,” the source said. ‘War crime’ The Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki described the strike as a “cowardly terrorist attack” against a civilian facility. “The cowardly terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia… which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” he said in a statement on X. US ‘may’ join Saudi strikes Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, US President Donald Trump said: “We may.” He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in Saudi Arabia “not acceptable”. US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for US military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed. Embassy warnings The Yemen conflict flared back to life after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle Eastern war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets. The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war in the region. Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen’s government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour’s civil war. Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy. The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware of attacks” on Riyadh airport on Saturday and called on American citizens to avoid the area. The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Spain’s embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a “new attack… by the Houthis”. A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies “indicated that they had decided to prohibit their staff’s travel to/from Riyadh Airport over the next week as a prudential step”. Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station. Yemen fighting Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-led government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP . The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country’s entire western coastline in a lightning offensive. The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area — a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping — but they claimed to have repelled the assault. Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Info minister alleges 'nexus' between PTI-led KP govt, terrorists. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Sunday alleged that the PTI-led government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre explained that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. The press conference by government ministers — Tarar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, and Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry — came shortly after the Centre imposed emergency in KP, citing the provincial government’s lack of efforts to combat terrorism. The Centre and the PTI — which was in power in KP — have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . Addressing the media in Islamabad, the information minister said all cabinet members who attended Sunday’s meeting were of the view that the “PTI government in KP is hand in glove with terrorists and has an unholy alliance with terrorists”. “Terrorists have a clear say in how each district will be run,” he alleged, citing reports from the Intelligence Bureau and law enforcement agencies (LEAs). He contended that while other political parties faced terrorist attacks in the region, the PTI got “secure access and passage” thanks to its alleged alliance with such groups. “What is the reason that even police stations of some districts have been sublet to the Taliban?” Tarar asked, emphasising that the case was not merely of inaction and incompetence but of “empowering” the terrorists. The minister went on to allege that a “power-sharing formula was gradually taking shape between terrorists and the PTI’s KP government, which was starting from southern districts and was ingressing further into the entire KP”. He said the “unholy alliance and the nexus between them, as a result of which they had outsourced several districts to terrorists,” enabled the martyrdom of people and attacks on civilian infrastructure. “I say this publicly that these [Taliban] are foreign-funded people who want to bring our country to destruction,” he said, asserting that a provincial government’s facilitation towards such elements was a “constitutional breakdown”. Tarar referred to the recent bill regarding police assignments and alleged that the KP government wanted to “hire individuals from terrorist groups in the police”. “They were gradually dragging the entire province towards destruction, irrefutable proof and evidence of which is available.” KP Advisory Council formed The minister then questioned the KP cabinet’s performance, hailed “riddance from this group” and provided details of a technocratic KP Advisory Council. The 11-member council has been formed by the Centre as part of the emergency measures under Article 232 of the Constitution, according to an order seen by Dawn . It will assist the governor in exercising the functions of the KP government on behalf of the federal government. Through the order, the Centre also appointed Advocate Sanaullah as the KP advocate general. The province’s home affairs will be overseen by former prisons chief Kifayatullah Khan, described as “very competent” by Tarar. Tariq Mahmood Pasha, a former FBR chief and an aide to then-finance minister Ishaq Dar, has been assigned as advisor for finance affairs. MNA Samar Haroon Bilour has been appointed as information adviser, while retired Lt Gen Nigar Johar has been tasked with health affairs. Former advocate general Amir Javed was assigned the portfolio for law; ex-senator Osman Saifullah Khan will advise the governor on energy and power; Asif Rafiq Afridi was given the portfolio for communication and works; while Maulana Tayyab Qureshi will oversee religious affairs. Tarar noted that all chosen advisers had either doctorate degrees or extensive experience in public service. These included Adviser for Industries and Commerce Dr Muhammad Irshad (a former FBR chief with a PhD in finance), Adviser for Mines and Minerals Dr Sarfraz Ali Shah (who had a PhD in economics) and Adviser for Education Dr Syed Amir Abdullah (with a PhD in international relations). The Cabinet Division has issued an order by the federal government that said that after the proclamation of an emergency, the government of KP “cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution”. Exercising its powers under Article 232, the government ordered that an Area Development Secretariat (ADS), under the superintendence of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC), be immediately established to “restore law and order, safeguard the security of the citizens of Pakistan and ensure good governance and development” in Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, South Waziristan (Upper) and South Waziristan (Lower). It said that the ARDC shall be a representative council comprising the notables from the designated districts and shall be headed by a chairman. The members, the chairman, the vice chairman and the spokesperson of the ARDC shall be appointed in such manner and for such duration, as may be determined. The order further said that the ADS shall be headed by the additional chief secretary of the designated Districts, who shall be the administrator of these areas. “Officials of the provincial government and of other bodies or authorities posted in the designated districts shall be placed under the operational and administrative control of ADS. Any further postings/transfers to the designated districts may be ordered by the prime minister on the recommendation of the administrator, from time to time,” it said. It said that the administrator shall perform all the functions of and exercise all executive, administrative, and law enforcement powers vested in or exercisable by the provincial government in the designated districts. It said that the administrator may: establish organisational setups for governance, security and development in selected districts with command over district administration, law enforcement and all line departments; issue binding orders to civil, police, and military authorities; issue orders for operational, organisational and administrative functions of ADS; issue orders for allocation and transfer of funds; coordinate with federal agencies, armed forces and provincial bodies for law enforcement and security of the areas; reorganise departments and take necessary actions for public safety, economic stability, relief operations and provision of essential services; and take such other measures as are necessary for the purposes of effective and good governance, maintenance of law and order and provision of services in the designated districts. “All orders, notifications, directions, or actions taken by the administrator shall have the same legal effect as if issued by the provincial government,” it read. Naqvi details govt efforts to resolve issues In his remarks, the interior minister said the Centre tried to take the KP government on board in the counterterrorism fight, but the efforts were in vain due to a lack of response from the latter. At the outset of Sunday’s briefing, Naqvi said, “Today was not an easy day for us. For over one month, we continuously tried to take the KP government on board. I was personally in touch with them in the background; our only goal was to onboard them so that we could fight together against terrorism.” The minister went on to reveal that he was in contact with PTI leaders until 11:45pm last night and had been communicating with them “all day about the draft’s para four”. “They did not respond all day.” “I told them that we can still avoid the situation. Things have gone too far, but we can still do something to delay tomorrow morning’s situation,” he said, referring to the imposition of emergency that the Centre had been mulling. Naqvi also highlighted efforts by veteran politician Maulana Fazlur Rehman to reduce tensions, but no solution could be found. He even said the Centre communicated to the PTI repeatedly that it had “no issue” with the party’s long march. “Our issue was entirely terrorism-related, and we want to take you on board on it.” While acknowledging that there were many issues related to KP’s governance, Naqvi said, “My and the entire interior ministry’s point of view was clear: the situation was not linked to politics even one per cent. We were purely seeing this on the basis of terrorism.” Referring to the Oct 3 talks between the Centre and PTI, he contended that the situation would have been different if they had reached an agreement back then.” “Even if last night they had said yes, it (emergency) would not have happened.” He added, “Ask them who their masterminds are. Who were sabotaging them?” The interior minister then elaborated on the security challenges KP faces, stating that the situation was “really bad” in 12 districts. “In some districts, you cannot even leave your house in the evening.” “We had multiple meetings with Sohail Afridi, and the only topic was terrorism; no political conversation happened,” he emphasised. The minister said a plan was proposed to strengthen KP Police in five districts initially and eventually hand over security to it in six months, then repeat the process in another five districts. “They said they had a lack of funds, but it is on the record that we said that we will provide any more funds you need. This was a four-month-old conversation but still no work has happened on it.” Naqvi further claimed that the PTI team had agreed on imposing emergency in 12 districts, but added that they were “scared of being seen meeting with us”. “We had clarity on one thing that we did not want to involve politics in this.” He further alleged, “Their connections with the Taliban are no secret. I would not say anything further.” The minister remarked that the security situation was extremely bad in certain districts, yet the PTI was able to hold rallies and “not even one person was harmed”. “We only had two options: either we would see the martyrdoms daily, or we end them. So this difficult decision we have made has a background,” he maintained, adding that the federal government tried its best to avoid it. During the briefing, Naqvi claimed that “demands” the PTI put forward were already being considered last month, before the opposition party announced its long march towards Islamabad. “Some of their own people could not understand why the long march was taking place.” He recalled that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif wanted to hold talks with the National Assembly opposition leader last month and proposed forming a committee, but the government did not get any confirmation. “We were trying our best to hold the meeting before the prime minister left so that the situation could be diffused,” he said, noting that a committee for the Oct 3 talks was formed later. According to the interior minister, the consultations took place for two days and credited PTI MNA Asad Qaiser for saying with “clarity that it is not possible that we take even a step back on terrorism”. “We will not do it for you; we will do it for Pakistan, and we will fight united against terrorism,” Naqvi quoted Qaiser as saying, adding that he requested the ex-NA speaker to take the KP government on board. The minister then reiterated that an agreement draft was revised four times, after which the government negotiation committee found out a new draft had been presented by the opposition team. “Although the previous day the chief minister had authorised them to agree on their behalf, the next day it all changed,” Naqvi said.

Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. The New Forever War mloukili Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:38 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 1 minutes The New Forever War Originally published in Foreign Affairs Why America and Iran Fight On Without Victory Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Ali Vaez Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/AliVaez Related Tags Iran United States When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another. Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce. The full article can be read on the Foreign Affairs website. South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 11:07 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Africa 29 September 2026 2 minutes South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech examines how President Kiir’s call for fresh elections aims to weaken his opponents, and may pave the way to worsening armed conflict Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Daniel Akech Senior Analyst, South Sudan https://twitter.com/jongethon Related Tags South Sudan South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir on 22 September dissolved the transitional unity government, established under a 2018 peace deal, declaring that the country would now prepare for long-delayed elections in December. But with the feasibility of holding the polls in doubt and fighting between government and rebel forces continuing in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, the move in effect serves to further concentrate power in the hands of Kiir and his family. Kiir’s move followed the adoption by parliament, which is loyal to the president, of a controversial amendment to the National Elections Act on 21 September, authorising the creation of a caretaker government. This amendment gave Kiir the opportunity to remove his five vice presidents – many of whom were appointed under the 2018 deal, including his perennial arch-rival, First Vice President Riek Machar. The government had already placed Machar, who led the rebel forces in the five-year civil war that ended in 2018, under house arrest in March last year, charging him with treason . State and rebel forces have been fighting since then, threatening to thrust South Sudan back into internecine conflict. Its last civil war is estimated to have cost nearly 400,000 lives and displaced more than four million people. President Kiir further marginalised rival factions and opposition elements in his caretaker government. His newly appointed ministers are almost entirely loyalists, whereas the Nuer – South Sudan’s second-largest ethnic group, to which Machar belongs – remain heavily underrepresented. There are now three Nuer cabinet ministers out of a total of 17, even after the president added additional appointees on 28 September. Kiir also appointed powerful figures from the security forces to become caretaker governors in key states, such as James Koang Chuol in Upper Nile, Moses Majok Gatluak in Jonglei and Rin Tueny Mabor in Lakes. Some political leaders have denounced the unrepresentative make-up of the new administration and rejected the changes. Kiir’s moves set up two potential scenarios. One is a rush to stage-manage snap elections, the first of their kind since the country’s independence in 2011, which could end up re-electing Kiir despite questions as to whether credible polls are even possible without an updated census, voter registry or dedicated funding. A mismanaged vote could also spark fresh rebellions or political violence. Alternatively, Kiir could delay elections yet again on technical grounds, effectively extending his term without the baggage of the 2018 accord’s power-sharing arrangements. Kiir is using an “inter-party dialogue” that started on 24 September to validate plans for elections in December or negotiate such an extension. Either way, Kiir’s moves have triggered alarm among the South Sudanese political elite that his aim is to consolidate power with the goal of managing a dynastic succession . His daughter Adut Kiir is now his most powerful aide, while his son Atem Salva Kiir oversees the presidential guard. Meanwhile, the new rebellion by Machar’s forces looks unlikely to subside as long as its leader remains on trial and under arrest. The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 18:14 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iraqi security forces stand guard during a funerary procession for a slain member of Iraq's Hashed al-Shaabi, or the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), who was killed in a US-Israeli air strike in Mosul the previous evening, in Baghdad on March 8, 2026. AHMAD AL-RUBAYE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 14 minutes The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? The coming withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces marks a significant moment in Iraq’s tumultuous recent history. Yet with the Middle East war bringing conflict to the country and questions surrounding the state’s capacity to assert its authority, the significance is mainly symbolic. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Iraq United States On 30 September, the U.S.-led coalition formed to fight the Islamic State (ISIS) is due to end its military mission in Iraq. While some had expected that the withdrawal of personnel and removal of materiel might slip beyond the scheduled date, it now appears that they will be completed on time. The largest remaining contingent is from the United States, which has maintained the biggest troop presence throughout. Several other coalition countries already have pulled out their smaller garrisons, including Poland, which completed its drawdown in March, and Germany , whose soldiers left in August. The departure closes a chapter that began in 2014, when ISIS seized large parts of the country and U.S.-led forces – which had previously invaded and occupied Iraq in 2003 and then withdrawn in 2011 – returned at Baghdad’s invitation. A number of Iraqi armed groups that first formed to combat ISIS came to cast the coalition as a threat. Aligned with Iran, these groups long invoked the coalition’s presence as a justification for keeping weapons and command structures outside the Iraqi state. With coalition forces on their way out, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has declared that these groups must now disarm. But the coalition is leaving amid a Middle East war sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, in which Tehran and some of its aligned groups based in Iraq have launched attacks on U.S. targets in Gulf Arab countries, Jordan and Iraq’s own Kurdistan region. The question is whether Baghdad can and will use the end of this foreign military mission to gain greater control of armed actors who – whatever justification they may offer – have reasons for fighting that extend well beyond opposition to the coalition’s presence. The End of a Mission The U.S.-led Global Coalition to Defeat the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria – dubbed Operation Inherent Resolve by the U.S. military – is ending its mission twelve years after its establishment. At that time, in 2014, a marauding ISIS had capitalised on the instability that gripped much of the Arab world following the 2011 uprisings, helped by the acquisition of conventional weapons from Iraqi and Syrian forces that quickly retreated from major cities such as Mosul and Raqqa in the face of the group’s onslaught. It exploited growing sectarian tensions in Iraq and perceptions of political exclusion among its Sunni Arab population to seize much of the country’s Sunni Arab heartland. In June 2014, ISIS declared a caliphate in Iraq and Syria and at its height, in May 2015, controlled as much as a third of Iraqi territory. Having terminated the U.S. occupation of Iraq only three years earlier, then-U.S. President Barack Obama decided to send troops back to prevent ISIS from expanding further and reverse its gains in both countries. In the ensuing years, the U.S. and dozens of coalition partners supported military operations against the group in both Iraq and Syria at the same time as they sought to help rebuild and train the Iraqi army, which had collapsed in a matter of days after the ISIS offensive. While the Iraqi government declared victory over ISIS as early as December 2017, having retaken Mosul and other key cities from ISIS control and secured its border with Syria, the coalition endured. It remained in the country even after March 2019, when the final ISIS stronghold in Baghouz, Syria fell; that loss marked the end of the group’s control of the last bit of the territory it had grabbed since beginning its 2014 offensive. The coalition – which included sizeable contingents from France, the UK and Türkiye in addition to the U.S. – stayed on for several reasons. First, it continued to support Iraqi armed forces suppressing residual ISIS cells for years after the recapture of Baghouz. The Iraqi army and Kurdish region’s armed forces ( peshmerga ) continued to suffer occasional hit-and-run attacks in the so-called disputed territories, an area claimed by both the federal and regional governments, whose rugged terrain offered ISIS fighters plenty of hideouts. As late as August 2024, U.S. troops operating alongside Iraqi forces sustained injuries during a raid on an ISIS cell in Anbar province. Secondly, the coalition used Iraq as a base from which to conduct operations against the group and others across the border in Syria, where a civil war raged for years, and where the U.S. partnered with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) until April. The ISIS danger appears to have significantly receded. Despite occasional attacks by its remnants, the group has lost its ideological traction. Though some people in both Iraq and Syria continue to harbour the grievances that ISIS played upon to galvanise support, few want to relive the era of the so-called caliphate, which triggered years of conflict and destroyed many of the communities the group ostensibly sought to protect. Moreover, the security gaps that ISIS exploited in 2014 have also narrowed in both countries. Syria’s new authorities have yet to establish full control of the country’s provinces and borders, but the process of integrating the previously autonomous SDF in the north east under the central government’s command is helping secure areas that remain vulnerable to ISIS. In Iraq, state forces are better prepared to repel any domestic or external threat the group might pose. Though the coalition and the Iraqi government share the assessment that Iraqi forces can counter ISIS on their own, the withdrawal is also politically expedient for both Baghdad and Washington. For years, despite its cooperation with coalition forces, Baghdad viewed their presence as a liability, not least because Iran-aligned armed groups seized on it to claim that the U.S. occupation was continuing. Those groups also accused the U.S. of using its foothold in Iraq to monitor Iran and the “axis of resistance” – its partners in the region. This latter charge became a justification for the Iraqi groups to retain their arms and command structures independent from the Iraqi state forces. Domestic political dynamics on the U.S. side may not have been as clear-cut, but they nevertheless militated for withdrawal. Trump was never the pure non-interventionist that he seemed to tout himself as being, but he has long sounded off against the Iraq war (a key theme of his 2016 campaign) and had already considered withdrawing from Syria during his first term. Despite his growing penchant for military intervention in his second term, Trump has continued to inveigh against endless U.S. wars, notably in the Middle East. Departing from Iraq is thus consistent both with the president’s longstanding rhetoric and also the views of significant parts of his political base. To the extent that Washington had contended that the coalition remained in Iraq at its government’s request, Baghdad’s desire for a troop withdrawal has for some time been a complication. Lastly, as a U.S. official noted to Crisis Group, amid the war with Iran, withdrawal would have the added benefit of reducing readily accessible U.S. targets for Tehran. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. In theory, the withdrawal should mark a milestone in Iraq’s relationship with the U.S. and its long road to normalcy following the chaos and violence that have plagued the country since the 2003 U.S. invasion. A series of Iraqi governments have desired to forge bilateral security cooperation agreements on Iraq’s own terms and with countries of its choosing. Baghdad can now strike these deals, not only with the U.S., but also with other former coalition partners such as the UK and France. But however politically necessary it may have deemed the withdrawal, Baghdad will hardly be able to sell the coalition’s departure as a celebratory moment, given that it coincides with the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which has turned Iraq into a battleground. Instead, the withdrawal’s timing will focus further attention on that conflict’s spillover effects. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. The fears of many Iraqis are therefore presently not centred around the risk of a resurgent ISIS but rather around Iran-aligned domestic groups that, in solidarity with their “axis of resistance” partners, and notwithstanding the U.S. withdrawal, may take action in defiance of the government’s policy of neutrality in the U.S.-Iran war, and thereby provoke military retaliation by outside actors. Some of the complications that the withdrawal could present for the Iraqi-U.S. relationship would have been difficult to anticipate when the drawdown timeline was conceived. That happened at another tense moment, following the outbreak of the Gaza war, when U.S. backing for Israel’s brutal military response to Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks undermined public support for bilateral close ties. In September 2024, when Zaidi’s predecessor Mohammed Shia’ al-Sudani was prime minister and Joe Biden was U.S. president, Baghdad and Washington agreed on a phased end to the coalition’s military mission. It would start with the coalition’s withdrawal from bases in federal Iraq by September 2025, to be followed by the final withdrawal from the Kurdistan region by the next 30 September. Now, with the U.S.-Iran war as backdrop, the withdrawal may well attract less attention as an indicator of the country’s recovery from ISIS than as a test of whether its government can repair Iraq’s battered sovereignty and protect its internal security at a moment of regional crisis. Reining In Armed Groups Zaidi has declared that the end of the coalition mission should mark the beginning of disarmament for groups that operate independently of the state. He has set June 2027 as the deadline for its completion. His political argument is straightforward: once the coalition troops are gone, the armed factions should no longer be able to invoke their presence as grounds for maintaining separate military structures. As he announces the mission’s conclusion on 30 September, he is expecting some of the factions to welcome a development that meets their longstanding demand and to reciprocate with their own commitment to cease hostilities. But not all of the armed groups will do so, given the variations among them and the dynamics created by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The Popular Mobilisation Forces, or Hashd al-Shaabi, emerged as a collection of Shiite armed groups assembled to fight ISIS and were subsequently nominally incorporated into Iraq’s formal security apparatus, with many retaining independent chains of command. They do not form a single faction and have very different relationships with Tehran. Not all have engaged in attacks outside Iraq’s borders. Some groups, such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq, appear willing to negotiate their future relationship with the state. Others, including factions associated with the self-described Islamic Resistance in Iraq, such as Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, are tied ideologically and operationally to Iran’s regional network. Their opposition to the U.S. extends well beyond the presence of coalition troops in Iraq, and they have served as a valuable vector for Iranian power projection. It is these latter factions that have participated in the Middle East war, striking U.S.-linked targets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries, including Jordan, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Their actions have strained Baghdad’s relations with Gulf states and, as noted, exposed Iraq to military retaliation by both the U.S. and Saudi Arabia. Zaidi thus has good reasons of his own to want to curb them, as his government cannot credibly reassure its neighbours, attract investment or pursue a foreign policy of neutrality while armed actors make decisions on war and peace independently of its will. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. They also are almost certain to take far longer than Zaidi’s deadline allows. If the talks stall, Zaidi could face U.S. pressure to use force against groups that earlier prime ministers were reluctant to confront militarily, fearing an intra-Shiite conflict and friction with Iran. In a mid-September interview , Zaidi said groups continuing to function as separate militias would be considered outlaws. He has yet to specify what action the government would take to corral those that defy him. As long as Tehran relies on close Iraqi partners in its war with the U.S., these groups have reason to preserve their military autonomy and may seek to prolong negotiations without relinquishing their arms. Even after the coalition’s withdrawal, they will likely point to other foreign security relationships, including Türkiye’s garrison in northern Iraq, to defend their stance. Some have also argued that any disarmament plan must simultaneously address the status of the Kurdish region’s peshmerga, although the parallel is inapt: peshmerga forces are governed by a specific law under the Iraqi constitution regarding federal regions’ responsibility to organise their own internal and border security. The government therefore ought to distinguish between forces operating under recognised state or regional authority, and factions conducting attacks without any such justification. The Kurdish Region’s Vulnerabilities The coalition’s departure has particular significance in the Kurdistan region, where its forces have supported the peshmerga and where U.S. troops remained even after leaving other bases in Iraq in September 2025. Erbil is not happy to see them depart. Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described withdrawal at this moment as “ shameful ”, no doubt because he is concerned about how to manage the threat posed by Iran and Iran-aligned groups, which have systematically targeted the region since the war began in February. Some of the strikes appear to have been motivated by the presence of U.S. forces, in line with attacks on other nearby countries hosting U.S. bases. But the near-daily strikes also have often hit Iraqi-based Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and were described by a Kurdish official to Crisis Group as a warning to Kurdistan to keep those groups out of the current conflict. Certainly, the coalition’s withdrawal will exacerbate vulnerabilities. Coalition forces based in Erbil provided the region with some level of air defence. Their impending departure will mean the loss of those capabilities, further exposing the region to missile and drone attack. The Kurdish official noted to Crisis Group that worries about the withdrawal were “not just about security and protection, but the message this sends to our adversaries”, reflecting fears that Iran and others will see the U.S. drawdown as an indication that they would no longer take a significant interest in the region’s future. Still, U.S. support will not necessarily dry up entirely, even if the basis for it will change. To date, U.S. support for the peshmerga has been governed by a memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, first signed in 2016 and last renewed in 2022 . But though the U.S. does not wish to extend the agreement, Kurdish authorities will continue to press Washington and other coalition partners for aid in the form of strikes, intelligence sharing, training and equipment – none of which necessarily requires a troop presence inside Iraq – as well as broader reassurance of assistance in facing the military threat from Iran and the groups that it backs. It may help that the regional government announced in September its completion of a peshmerga reorganisation sought by the U.S. and agreed to in the lapsing memorandum. But future cooperation will require further work to define the terms on which Baghdad, Erbil and foreign partners will operate. Erbil and Baghdad, whose relationship has traditionally been fraught, will surely have to work together more closely. That said, at least for now, Kurdish officials say they are impressed with Zaidi and believe he is sincere in his stated intention of trying to tackle the militia problem. Looking Ahead When Trump returned to the White House for his second term, much of his base hoped and believed that his administration would avoid military adventurism and seek to extract the country from strategic quagmires. Some of his personnel decisions, particularly at the Pentagon, seemed to lend credence to such speculation, as did the foreign policy views of his vice president, JD Vance. Officials who sought to pursue a more restraint-oriented foreign policy or to concentrate on competition with China by downsizing other overseas commitments were not a dominant force within the new administration but nevertheless held key positions. Both of these groups favoured reassessing U.S. force posture in the Middle East, particularly the legacy missions in both Iraq and Syria. Whatever influence these camps have, their perspectives have not guided key foreign policy decisions in Trump’s latest year in office, which has been characterised by aggressive unilateralism and reliance on military force as a tool of statecraft. But the trajectory of U.S. policy on Iraq and Syria is an exception to that trend. Administration sources tell Crisis Group that, buoyed by the unexpected ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in Syria, key U.S. officials, particularly at the Pentagon, pushed to reassess the U.S. troop presence there and prevailed in a series of internal policy debates on the matter. Those efforts were boosted when it became clear how vulnerable U.S. troops in the region had become as a result of the conflict with Iran. U.S. officials also have positive views of Zaidi, who visited Washington in July and was received warmly by Trump. They are particularly pleased by Zaidi’s pledges on armed group disarmament. Even those who are sceptical of how those efforts will fare appreciate the Iraqi prime minister’s tone and confidence. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. A prolonged conflict is likely to lead Iran to enlist its partners in Iraq to use the country as a staging ground for significant attacks on the interests of the U.S. and its regional partners. That in turn would inevitably undermine the bilateral relationship and could trigger retaliatory U.S. moves at a time when Washington still enjoys outsized influence, including because it controls a significant portion of Iraq’s oil proceeds, which are deposited in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Trump administration has already twice used the leverage the oil revenue affords the U.S. in pressing Iraq to take more proactive measures to dilute Iran’s influence. For now, Zaidi’s ascension has eased strains, and the U.S. withdrawal gives him an argument for reining in armed groups. That may be enough for him to make progress with some of the groups, but doubters are right to question how far he will be able to go. Indeed, it would be entirely unrealistic to expect that Baghdad can compel the surrender of weapons or severing of ties with Iran forged through years of regional conflict. The symbolism of 30 September is significant, but in the end Iraq’s stability will depend more on whether the U.S. gives it the time and space required to bring armed groups under its central authority, and whether Baghdad and Washington work together to protect Iraq from the worst effects of the U.S.-Iranian confrontation in the meantime.
